questions.question: What is a Bloom filter used for in databases?

options.text: Quickly checking if an element is definitely NOT in a set

questions.explanation: Bloom filter is a probabilistic data structure. It can say 'definitely not in set' (no false negatives) or 'possibly in set' (false positives possible). Used to avoid expensive disk lookups for non-existent keys.

questions.question: How do Bloom filters help LSM-tree databases like Cassandra?

options.text: They avoid reading SSTables that definitely don't contain the requested key

questions.explanation: LSM-trees have multiple SSTables. Without Bloom filters, a read might check all SSTables. Bloom filter for each SSTable quickly eliminates those that definitely don't have the key, reducing disk I/O.

questions.question: What is a B-tree?

options.text: A self-balancing tree optimized for disk-based storage with high fanout
A tree for storing binary data

questions.explanation: B-tree is a self-balancing tree with high fanout (many children per node). Optimized for disk: each node fits a disk page, minimizing I/O. Foundation of most relational database indexes.

questions.question: Why are B-trees preferred over binary trees for database indexes?

options.text: B-trees have lower height due to high fanout, reducing disk I/O
Binary trees don't support range queries

questions.explanation: B-trees have high fanout (hundreds of children per node), keeping tree height low (typically 3-4 levels for millions of records). Each level = one disk read. Binary trees would be much deeper, requiring more I/O.

questions.question: What is an LSM-tree (Log-Structured Merge-tree)?

options.text: A write-optimized structure that buffers writes in memory and periodically merges to disk

questions.explanation: LSM-tree optimizes writes: data goes to in-memory buffer (memtable), then flushes to immutable sorted files (SSTables) on disk. Background compaction merges SSTables. Used by Cassandra, RocksDB, LevelDB.

questions.question: Which workload pattern benefits most from LSM-trees?
questions.explanation: LSM-trees excel at write-heavy workloads: all writes are sequential (append to log/memtable), avoiding random disk I/O. Reads may need to check multiple SSTables, making them slower than B-trees for reads.

questions.question: What is 'write amplification' in LSM-trees?

options.text: Data being written multiple times due to compaction

questions.explanation: Write amplification: data is written multiple times—first to memtable/WAL, then to SSTable, then rewritten during compaction. A single logical write may result in 10-30x physical writes. Trade-off for write optimization.

questions.question: What is the difference between B-tree and B+ tree?

options.text: B+ tree stores data only in leaf nodes; B-tree stores in all nodes

questions.explanation: B+ tree stores actual data only in leaf nodes; internal nodes contain only keys for navigation. Leaves are linked for efficient range scans. Most database indexes use B+ trees, not pure B-trees.

questions.question: True or False: Bloom filters can have false negatives.
questions.explanation: Bloom filters never have false negatives: if it says 'not in set', the element is definitely not there. They can have false positives: 'possibly in set' might be wrong. This property makes them useful for filtering.

questions.question: What is compaction in LSM-tree databases?

options.text: Merging multiple SSTables into fewer, larger ones while removing duplicates and deleted data

questions.explanation: Compaction merges SSTables: combines sorted files, removes obsolete versions and tombstones (deleted data), and produces fewer, larger files. Essential for read performance and space reclamation in LSM-trees.

questions.question: Which databases use LSM-trees? (Choose all that apply)
questions.explanation: Cassandra, RocksDB, and LevelDB use LSM-trees for write optimization. PostgreSQL uses B-trees for indexes. LSM-trees are common in NoSQL and embedded databases optimized for write-heavy workloads.

questions.question: What is a 'tombstone' in LSM-tree databases?

options.text: A marker indicating a deleted record, removed during compaction

questions.explanation: LSM-trees are append-only; deletes write a tombstone marker. During reads, tombstones indicate deleted data. Compaction removes tombstones and the data they mark, reclaiming space.
